summary: Fluency within 1000 is adaptive strategy choice, not just faster column arithmetic: pupils match the most efficient method to the particular numbers. The child should hold three tools and pick well — the standard columnar algorithm (for problems where no shortcut helps, e.g. 456+287), mental strategies (compensation 525+199 = 525+200-1, near-doubles, place-value partitioning), and counting up on an empty number line for close subtractions (300-298, 401-399). Subtraction is linked to addition for checking (inverse), not re-counting. Learners also need to handle known systematic subtraction bugs: smaller-from-larger, and borrow/decompose across a zero.
misconceptions: Reaches for the column algorithm for every problem even when counting up or compensating is far quicker (strategy inflexibility)
Smaller-from-larger subtraction bug — subtracts the smaller digit from the larger in a column regardless of position
Cannot decompose to subtract when a column is zero (borrow-across-zero)
Treats subtraction as unrelated to addition — re-counts to check instead of using the inverse

activities.title: Two-track strategy bench: match the method to the numbers
steps: Meet a problem such as 300-298. Before computing, glance at the numbers and predict which method will be quickest.
Solve it two ways side by side: an empty-number-line track (count up from 298 to 300) and a column-algorithm track (set up and exchange across the zero). Time or step-count both.
Compare: on 300-298 the number line jumps the gap in one hop of 2 while the column track is still exchanging across the zero (and may trip over it).
Now try 456+287 the same way and compare: no obvious shortcut stands out for these numbers, so the column algorithm is a sensible, efficient choice here.

Add a check step using the inverse, with this activity's own numbers: for 300-298, add your answer (2) back to 298 and confirm you reach 300; for 456+287 (=743), subtract one addend from the total to recover the other.
activities.insight: Fluency means matching the method to the numbers, not grinding one algorithm; close numbers favour counting up, near-multiples favour compensation, and messy numbers favour the column algorithm.

activities.title: Sort first, then solve: which method would you choose?
steps: Sort 8 problems into three piles: 'count up' (close numbers), 'compensate' (near a multiple like +199), and 'column' (no shortcut helps).
For each problem, state in one phrase why it belongs in that pile ('these two are close, so I count up').

Transfer: given a new pair such as 502-5, decide which method is quickest — note the two numbers are far apart but only 5 is taken away, so counting back 5 or compensation beats a column borrow across the zero.
activities.insight: Strategy selection is a distinct, assessable skill: you can name and justify why a particular method fits particular numbers before doing any arithmetic.

activities.title: Fix the subtraction bugs: smaller-from-larger and borrow across zero
steps: Work 703-568 with base-ten materials (or place-value chips) before writing digits: exchange one hundred into ten tens, then one ten into ten ones, so 703 becomes 6 hundreds, 9 tens, 13 ones.
Check each column: confirm you cannot take 8 from 3 in the ones without exchanging — you do not simply subtract the smaller digit from the larger.
Complete the written algorithm, keeping the borrow moving left across the zero (the answer is 135).

Compare your answer with a wrong answer like 265 and explain which columns were mishandled (265 comes from taking the smaller digit from the larger in each column: the ones (3 take 8) and tens (0 take 6) skipped their exchanges, so the hundreds was never reduced from 7 to 6; the ones digit 5 matches the correct answer only by coincidence).
activities.insight: Column subtraction requires exchanging by place value; a top digit smaller than the bottom digit means you must decompose, and when a zero column must give to the column on its right (as in 703-568), it first needs an exchange from the hundreds — not leaving the column as 0.

activities.title: Strategy-menu reference and 'convince me' justification
steps: Build or use a strategy-menu wall with three worked examples, one per method (count up, compensate, column), each labelled with when it is the smart pick.
After solving a problem, explain to a partner or coach why your chosen method was quickest for those numbers.
Respond to a challenge ('convince me your method was quickest') by pointing to the number features that made your choice efficient.
activities.insight: Being able to articulate why a method fits particular numbers consolidates adaptive expertise and exposes whether a choice was reasoned or habitual.

checkQuestion: Put these four in front of the child one at a time and say: 'Solve each one however you think is best, and tell me why you chose that way.' 300 - 298; 525 + 199; 456 + 287; 703 - 568. Watch WHICH method they reach for each time and listen to the 'why'.
checkAnswer: Flexible and fluent: solves 300-298 by counting up / difference of 2 (not columnar borrowing), adds 199 by 525+200-1 (compensation), uses the columnar algorithm for 456+287 where no shortcut helps, and handles 703-568 with a correct exchange across the zero. Justifies each choice by the numbers ('these two are close, so I counted up').
